passages.happening:
God tells Moses to collect twelve staffs, one from the leader of each tribe. “Write each man’s name on his staff, and write Aaron’s name on the staff of Levi” (verses 2-3). The staffs are to be placed in the tent ‘in front of the Testimony’ (verse 4).

God says what will happen. “The staff belonging to the man I choose will sprout, and I will rid Myself of the constant grumbling of the Israelites against you” (verse 5).

Moses does so. He sets the staffs before the LORD in the tent, and Aaron's staff is among them (verses 6-7).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 16 ended with judgment and with a plague stopped by Aaron's prayer. But judgment had not settled the question. The very day after the rebels died, the whole congregation was grumbling again. So God answers the question a second time, and this time with a sign of life.

A staff was more than a walking stick. It was a sign of authority, carried by leaders, shepherds and heads of households. It was personal enough to identify its owner: in Genesis, Judah's staff is used to prove who he is (Genesis 38:18).

There is a play on words that the first hearers would have caught at once. The Hebrew word for a staff, matteh, is also the word for a tribe. A tribe was the group under one leader's staff. So the question in the tent is, quite literally, which matteh God will choose. The word comes sixteen times in this short chapter.

The ‘Testimony’ is the name for the two stone tablets of the covenant, kept inside the ark. To put the staffs in front of the Testimony is to put them before the ark, in the innermost place. Whatever happens to them there, God will have done it.

Aaron's name is written on the staff of Levi. The test is fair. His staff is one dead stick among twelve.
passages.later:
Jeremiah was shown a branch of an almond tree at his calling, and God said, ‘I am watching over My word to accomplish it’ (Jeremiah 1:12). In Hebrew the words for almond and for watching sound alike.

Hebrews draws the lesson of this chapter for the priesthood: “No one takes this honor upon himself; he must be called by God, just as Aaron was” (Hebrews 5:4).
passages.asks: Each leader handed over his staff, the sign of his own standing, and left it with God overnight. Ask what standing or title of your own you would find it hard to lay down and leave in God's hands. And ask whether you want God to choose, or only to confirm what you have chosen.

passages.happening:
“The next day Moses entered the Tent of the Testimony and saw that Aaron’s staff, representing the house of Levi, had sprouted, put forth buds, blossomed, and produced almonds” (verse 8).

Moses brings all the staffs out. The Israelites look at them, and each leader takes back his own (verse 9). God tells Moses to put Aaron's staff back before the ark, ‘to be kept as a sign for the rebellious’, so that the grumbling will end, ‘lest they die’ (verse 10).

The people cry out to Moses, “Look, we are perishing! We are lost; we are all lost! Anyone who comes near the tabernacle of the LORD will die. Are we all going to perish?” (verses 12-13).
passages.hearers:
A staff is dead wood, cut from its tree long before. Verse 8 slows down and piles up four verbs: it sprouted, budded, blossomed and bore ripe almonds. The whole cycle of a growing season happened in one night, on a stick with no root.

The almond tree was among the first to flower in the land, late in winter. Its blossom was already part of Israel's worship. The cups of the golden lampstand in the tent were shaped like almond flowers (Exodus 25:33-34). So the sign matched the place where it was given.

Notice the difference from chapter 16. There God answered the challenge to Aaron with fire and an opened earth. The censers of the dead were hammered onto the altar as a warning. Here the answer is fruit, and Aaron's staff is kept before the ark as a witness. The priest God chooses is marked by life.

The other eleven leaders take their staffs home, still plain wood. Nothing has been done to them. They have only been shown which staff God made to flower.

God states the purpose of the sign in verse 10. It is to end the grumbling ‘lest they die’. The sign is meant to prevent more deaths.

But the people draw a different conclusion, and the chapter ends on their cry. After the earth, the fire and the plague, they have at last taken God's holiness seriously. Now they fear that no one can live near him at all. The cry is left hanging. Chapter 18 is God's reply.
passages.later:
Hebrews lists the staff among the things kept with the ark: “Inside the ark were the gold jar of manna, Aaron’s staff that had budded, and the stone tablets of the covenant” (Hebrews 9:4). By the time Solomon's temple was dedicated, only the tablets were there (1 Kings 8:9). What became of the staff is not known.

Christians have often seen a likeness between dead wood that bursts into life and the resurrection of Jesus. The New Testament does not draw that line itself, so it is best held as an echo and no more.

To the people's fear of coming near, the New Testament answers with an invitation: “let us draw near with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith” (Hebrews 10:22).
passages.hard:
Were the people right to fear that anyone who came near the tabernacle would die?

In one way they were. They had watched the earth swallow the rebels, fire burn up 250 men, and a plague kill thousands. Their fear shows that they had stopped treating God's presence lightly.

But their conclusion goes too far. God's purpose in the sign was to keep them alive (verse 10). And in the next chapter he answers their cry directly. He gives the priests and Levites the work of guarding the sanctuary, ‘so that wrath may not fall on the Israelites again’ (18:5).

Readers hear the cry in two ways. Some take it as a healthy turn from contempt to reverence. Others see a swing to despair, the opposite mistake from Korah's. Korah thought anyone could walk in. The people now think no one can.

The Bible's answer to the fear of a holy God is never to make God less holy. It is to provide someone to stand between: first Aaron and his sons, and in the end, the New Testament says, Christ.
passages.asks: The people swung from thinking God could be approached on any terms to thinking he could not be approached at all. Ask which of those two mistakes is nearer to your own. And ask whether you come to God with both reverence and confidence, or have let go of one of them.
